Octopuses have three hearts and blue blood.
An octopus has around 500 million neurons, most of them in its arms.
Cuttlefish can change colour even though they are thought to be colour-blind.
Squid and octopuses use copper-based haemocyanin, which turns their blood blue.
The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever lived.
A blue whale's heart can weigh around 180 kg.
Sperm whales have the largest brains of any animal.
Humpback whale songs can last for hours and change from year to year.
Orcas are the largest members of the dolphin family.
Dolphins sleep with one half of the brain at a time.
Bottlenose dolphins appear to use signature whistles that work like names.
Narwhal tusks are actually a long spiral tooth.
Belugas are nicknamed 'sea canaries' for their chirps and whistles.
Sea otters hold hands while sleeping so they don't drift apart.
Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal — up to a million hairs per square inch.
Walruses use their tusks to haul themselves out of the water onto ice.
Manatees are more closely related to elephants than to seals.
Polar bears have black skin under their see-through fur.
Polar bears are classed as marine mammals.
Emperor penguins can dive deeper than 500 m.
Emperor penguin dads balance the egg on their feet for about two months.
Penguins only live in the Southern Hemisphere (the Galápagos penguin just crosses the equator).
Gentoo penguins are the fastest swimming penguins, reaching about 35 km/h.
Little penguins, the smallest species, stand only about 30 cm tall.
Some penguins give pebbles to their partners when building nests.
Penguins drink seawater; a gland above their eyes removes the extra salt.
Flamingos are pink because of pigments in the algae and shrimp they eat.
A group of flamingos is called a flamboyance.
A group of crows is called a murder.
A group of owls is called a parliament.
A group of ferrets is called a business.
A group of jellyfish is called a smack.
Crows can recognise individual human faces and remember them for years.
New Caledonian crows make and use hooked tools.
Owls can't move their eyes, so they turn their heads up to about 270 degrees.
Hummingbirds are the only birds that can fly backwards.
A hummingbird's heart can beat more than 1,000 times a minute.
The peregrine falcon can exceed 300 km/h in a hunting dive.
The ostrich lays the largest eggs of any living bird.
Ostriches can run at about 70 km/h.
The Arctic tern has the longest migration of any animal, flying pole to pole every year.
Bar-tailed godwits can fly over 11,000 km without stopping.
Albatrosses can glide for hours without flapping their wings.
Parrots can live for decades — some species over 60 years.
Kea, a New Zealand parrot, are famous for pulling rubber off cars.
The kakapo is a flightless, nocturnal parrot from New Zealand.
Kiwi birds lay eggs that are huge relative to their body size.
Woodpeckers have tongues that wrap around their skulls.
Protein studies suggest T. rex was more closely related to chickens than to lizards.
Birds are living dinosaurs.
Elephants can recognise themselves in a mirror.
An elephant's trunk has tens of thousands of muscle units.
Elephants communicate with low rumbles that humans can't hear.
African elephants are the largest land animals alive today.
Giraffes have the same number of neck vertebrae as humans: seven.
A giraffe's tongue can be about 45–50 cm long.
Giraffes only need a few minutes of deep sleep at a time.
Each giraffe's coat pattern is unique.
Zebra stripes may help deter biting flies.
Hippos secrete a reddish substance that acts like sunscreen.
Hippos can't really swim — they walk or bounce along river bottoms.
Rhinos' horns are made of keratin, the same protein as human fingernails.
Cheetahs can reach about 100 km/h in short sprints.
Cheetahs can't roar; they purr and chirp instead.
Lions are the only cats that live in large social groups.
A lion's roar can be heard up to about 8 km away.
Tigers have striped skin, not just striped fur.
No two tigers have the same stripe pattern.
Snow leopards can't roar.
Jaguars have one of the strongest bites of any big cat relative to size.
Domestic cats spend a large part of their day sleeping.
A cat's purr vibrates at roughly 25–150 Hz.
Cats have a reflective layer behind their eyes that helps them see in dim light.
Dogs' noses have hundreds of millions of scent receptors.
A dog's nose print is unique, like a human fingerprint.
Bloodhounds can follow scent trails that are days old.
Grey wolves can travel tens of kilometres in a single day.
Wolves were domesticated into dogs more than 15,000 years ago.
Foxes use Earth's magnetic field to help aim their pounces, some studies suggest.
Arctic foxes change coat colour with the seasons.
Red pandas are not closely related to giant pandas.
Giant pandas spend up to 14 hours a day eating bamboo.
Giant pandas have a 'pseudo-thumb' — an enlarged wrist bone for gripping bamboo.
Koalas sleep up to around 20 hours a day.
Koalas have fingerprints that are remarkably similar to human ones.
Kangaroos can't easily walk backwards.
A baby kangaroo is called a joey.
Wombats produce cube-shaped droppings.
Platypuses are mammals that lay eggs.
Male platypuses have venomous spurs on their hind legs.
Echidnas are egg-laying mammals too.
Tasmanian devils have one of the strongest bites for their size of any mammal.
Quokkas are small marsupials famous for looking like they're smiling.
Sloths can take about a month to digest a single meal.
Sloths come down from trees roughly once a week to go to the toilet.
Algae can grow in sloth fur, giving them a greenish tint.
Nine-banded armadillos usually give birth to identical quadruplets.
Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight.
Vampire bats share blood meals with roost-mates who didn't feed.
Some bats can eat over a thousand insects in an hour.
Naked mole-rats rarely get cancer and can live over 30 years.
Capybaras are the largest rodents in the world.
Beavers' teeth are orange because they contain iron.
A beaver dam in Canada's Wood Buffalo National Park is long enough to spot in satellite images.
Squirrels forget where they buried many of their nuts, helping trees spread.
Rats laugh when tickled — in ultrasonic chirps.
Hedgehogs have around 5,000 to 7,000 spines.
Porcupine quills have tiny backward barbs.
Meerkats take turns standing guard while the group forages.
Honey badgers are famously fearless and will take on much larger animals.
Camels store fat, not water, in their humps.
A thirsty camel can drink over 100 litres of water in about ten minutes.
Llamas and alpacas are related to camels.
Reindeer are the only deer where both males and females usually grow antlers.
Reindeer eyes change colour from gold in summer to blue in winter.
Moose are the largest members of the deer family.
Bison are the heaviest land animals in North America.
European bison were saved from extinction partly through breeding in Białowieża.
Gorillas share about 98% of their DNA with humans.
Chimpanzees use sticks to fish for termites.
Orangutans spend most of their lives in trees.
Bonobos often resolve conflicts through social bonding rather than fighting.
Lemurs are found in the wild only on Madagascar.
Mandrills are the largest monkeys in the world.
Howler monkeys are among the loudest land animals.
Crocodiles have been around in recognisable form for tens of millions of years.
Crocodiles can't stick out their tongues.
Alligators are found in the wild only in the United States and China.
Saltwater crocodiles are the largest living reptiles.
Komodo dragons are the largest living lizards.
Chameleons' tongues can be longer than their bodies.
Geckos can walk on ceilings thanks to millions of tiny hairs on their toes.
Some lizards can shed and regrow their tails.
Horned lizards can squirt blood from their eyes to scare predators.
Green sea turtles get their name from the colour of their fat.
Leatherback turtles can dive deeper than 1,000 m.
Galápagos giant tortoises can live over 100 years.
Snakes smell with their tongues.
Some snakes can sense the heat of their prey with special pits on their face.
The reticulated python is the longest snake species.
The green anaconda is the heaviest snake species.
Ireland and New Zealand have no native land snakes.
Frogs absorb water through their skin.
Wood frogs can survive being partly frozen in winter.
The axolotl can regrow limbs, parts of its heart and even its spinal cord.
Axolotls stay in their larval form for life.
Glass frogs have see-through skin on their bellies.
The golden poison frog is one of the most toxic animals on Earth.
Sharks have been around for over 400 million years — longer than trees.
Sharks don't have bones; their skeletons are made of cartilage.
Whale sharks are the largest fish in the sea.
Greenland sharks may live for more than 250 years.
Hammerhead sharks' wide heads help them sense prey.
Seahorse fathers carry the eggs and give birth.
Clownfish are all born male; some later become female.
Electric eels can produce shocks of several hundred volts.
Electric eels are actually a kind of knifefish, not true eels.
Pufferfish can inflate by gulping water.
Many pufferfish contain tetrodotoxin, a powerful poison.
Flying fish can glide for more than 200 metres.
Salmon return to the river where they hatched to spawn.
Goldfish can remember things for months, not seconds.
Anglerfish use a glowing lure to attract prey in the dark.
Some deep-sea fish make their own light through bioluminescence.
Jellyfish have no brain, heart or bones.
One jellyfish species, Turritopsis dohrnii, can revert to an earlier life stage.
Box jellyfish have 24 eyes.
Starfish can regrow lost arms.
Starfish digest food by pushing their stomach out of their mouth.
Sea cucumbers can expel their internal organs to distract predators.
Corals are animals, not plants.
Sponges are among the simplest animals and have no organs.
Lobsters taste with their legs.
Mantis shrimp punch fast enough to break aquarium glass.
Mantis shrimp have far more types of colour receptors than humans.
Hermit crabs swap shells as they grow.
Horseshoe crabs have blue blood used to test medicines for contamination.
Krill are tiny crustaceans eaten by whales, seals and penguins.
Antarctic krill may be one of the most abundant animal species by total mass.
Tardigrades can survive extreme cold, radiation and even the vacuum of space.
Honeybees communicate the location of flowers with a waggle dance.
A honeybee makes about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in its lifetime.
Bumblebees can fly in cooler weather than many other bees.
Ants can carry many times their own body weight.
Leafcutter ants grow fungus gardens to eat.
Some ant colonies have millions of members.
Termite mounds have built-in ventilation systems.
Monarch butterflies migrate thousands of kilometres to Mexico.
Butterflies taste with their feet.
Moths far outnumber butterflies in species.
Dragonflies catch the vast majority of the prey they chase.
Fireflies make light with almost no heat.
Cockroaches can survive for a while without their heads.
Dung beetles can navigate using the Milky Way.
The bombardier beetle sprays a boiling chemical spray at attackers.
Mosquitoes find people partly by sensing the carbon dioxide we breathe out.
Only female mosquitoes bite.
Spiders are arachnids, not insects — they have eight legs.
Spider silk is, weight for weight, stronger than steel.
Some spiders travel through the air on silk threads, called ballooning.
Jumping spiders have excellent eyesight for their size.
Scorpions glow under ultraviolet light.
Earthworms breathe through their skin.
Snails can have thousands of tiny teeth.
Slugs and snails leave mucus trails that help them glide.
A leech's body has 32 segments, each with its own cluster of nerve cells.
Horses can sleep standing up.
Horses can't vomit.
Cows have one stomach with four compartments.
Goats have rectangular pupils.
Pigs are among the most intelligent domestic animals.
Sheep can recognise the faces of other sheep and of people.
Ducks have waterproof feathers thanks to an oil gland near their tail.
Swans mostly pair up for life.
Geese fly in V-formations to save energy.
Peacocks' famous tails are the males' long upper tail feathers.
The shoebill is a huge bird with a shoe-shaped beak.
Pelicans' throat pouches can hold more than their stomachs.
Puffins can hold many small fish in their beaks at once.
Snowy owls hunt during the day in the Arctic summer.
Arctic ground squirrels can drop their body temperature below freezing during hibernation.
Musk oxen have lived in the Arctic since the last Ice Age.
Lemmings don't actually jump off cliffs in mass suicides — that's a myth.
Narwhals live year-round in Arctic waters.
Leopard seals are top predators in Antarctic waters.
Weddell seals live farther south than any other mammal.
